papers.title_in_file: Computing with only a few light particles
papers.what_it_is: A Quantum Computing Inc educational web lesson explaining photons, number states versus coherent states, antibunching, and why weak coherent states are used as a testbed for few-photon photonic computing.

assertions.value: The lesson states that the energy of a photon of a given wavelength is fixed, and that the amount of light energy changes with the number of photons, so a brighter pulse of the same color contains more photons than a fainter one.
assertions.anchor: Photons, the particles that makeup light, paragraph 3
quotes: The amount of energy that a photon of a given wavelength (which determines its color) has is fixed, but the amount of energy can be changed by changing the number of photons.
A brighter pulse of light contains more photons than a fainter one which is the same color.
assertions.certainty_reason: The lesson states this as a basic definition-level fact of the setting.

assertions.value: The lesson gives lower energy use as an obvious motivation for computing with fewer photons.
assertions.anchor: Photons, the particles that makeup light, paragraph 3
quotes: This gives an obvious motivation to use fewer particles - it requires less energy.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor lesson states its motivation without a measurement.

assertions.value: The lesson states that if light were not composed of discrete particles, the rate of energy emission from hot objects would be infinite, a paradox it names the ultraviolet catastrophe, and that discretization fixes it.
assertions.anchor: Photons, the particles that makeup light, paragraph 1
quotes: If light wasn't composed of discrete particles, the rate of energy emission would be infinite, an apparent paradox known as the ultraviolet catastrophe.
This discretization fixes the apparent paradox
assertions.certainty_reason: Textbook physics restated in a vendor lesson without derivation or citation.

assertions.value: The lesson defines a number state as a pulse of light containing an exact number of photons, and states that with a perfect measurement device a number state with two photons always gives a result of exactly two.
assertions.anchor: Photons, the particles that makeup light, paragraph 4
quotes: A pulse of light which is represented by a number state contains an exact number of photons.
Assuming a perfect measurement device, a number state with two photons will always give a result of exactly two.
assertions.certainty_reason: The lesson defines the term in the text.

assertions.value: The lesson states that a coherent state has a fixed amount of energy and so a fixed average photon number, but that measurements are noisy even with a perfect device, with outcomes random as if each photon were added independently of the others (Poisson statistics).
assertions.anchor: Photons, the particles that makeup light, paragraph 4
quotes: There is a different kind of state, known as a coherent state, and these states have a fixed amount of energy.
This means there will be a fixed amount of photons on average, but measurements will be noisy.
The outcomes are random as if each photon has been added independently of the others (mathematically this is known as Poisson statistics ).
assertions.certainty_reason: The lesson defines coherent states and their measurement statistics in the text.

assertions.value: The lesson states that number states can only be built with integer numbers of photons, while coherent states can have an average photon number that is not an integer, and even less than one.
assertions.anchor: Photons, the particles that makeup light, paragraph 4
quotes: It is therefore only possible to build number states with integer numbers of photons, but coherent states can be made with an average number of photons that are not an integer, and even less than one.
assertions.certainty_reason: The lesson states this as a property of the two state types it defines.

assertions.value: The lesson states that, no matter how few photons a weak coherent state has, it behaves like a classical pulse of light until the final measurement, which must measure an integer number of photons.
assertions.anchor: Photons, the particles that makeup light, paragraph 4
quotes: A remarkable fact about weak coherent states is that no matter how few photons they have, they still behave like a classical pulse of light until the final measurement, which must measure an integer number of photons.
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement in a vendor lesson with no derivation in the page.

assertions.value: The lesson states that weak coherent states are relatively easy to produce, and so provide a good starting point for developing technology.
assertions.anchor: Photons, the particles that makeup light, last sentences
quotes: Weak coherent states are relatively easy to produce, so as we see later, they provide a good starting point for developing technology.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor describes its own development approach.

assertions.value: The lesson states that, for a perfect detector, detecting a photon can only make it more likely, not less, that another is detected soon after under classical light, so that a beam of constant brightness gives the most spread out detections and any intensity profile only makes the distribution more bunched.
assertions.anchor: It is easier to see quantum mechanics with fewer particles, paragraph 2
quotes: For a perfect detector, detecting a photon can only ever make it more likely that we detect another one soon after, not less.
no matter what the intensity profile looks like, the probability peaks at a time difference of zero and the most spread out they can be is if the intensity is uniform.
assertions.certainty_reason: Illustrated by an animation in a vendor lesson; no proof in the text.

assertions.value: The lesson defines antibunched light as light in which detecting a photon makes it less likely to detect another one right after, and states that evenly spaced single light particles are the way to make light very antibunched, indicating the quantum nature of single photon states. It cites an early experiment that observed antibunching in light from a quantum source.
assertions.anchor: It is easier to see quantum mechanics with fewer particles, paragraph 2
quotes: There is a kind of light known as antibunched light that is less likely to detect a photon right after detecting another one.
This early experiment was able to observe antibunching in light from a quantum source.
It should be intuitive that evenly spaced single light particles are the way to make light very antibunched indicating the quantum nature of single photon states.
assertions.certainty_reason: The experiment is cited by link text only; the lesson gives no detail of the result.

assertions.value: The lesson states that, as the number of photons in a number state increases, the second-order coherence approaches, but never quite reaches, the minimum value that classical light can take.
assertions.anchor: It is easier to see quantum mechanics with fewer particles, paragraph 3
quotes: This states that as the number of photons in a number state increases, this quantity approaches, but never quite reaches, the minimum value that classical light can take.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated without a derivation or a value in the text.

assertions.value: The lesson states that adding more particles, even in a very quantum way, masks the fact that they are discrete particles, and that quantum states with a single photon or few photons are an excellent environment to realize quantum effects. It uses an analogy of grains of sand.
assertions.anchor: It is easier to see quantum mechanics with fewer particles, paragraph 3
quotes: Adding more particles, even in a very quantum way, masks the fact that they are discrete particles.
Quantum states (as opposed to coherent states, and including but not limited to number states) with a single or few photons are an excellent environment to realize quantum effects
assertions.certainty_reason: An argument by analogy in a vendor lesson, with no measurement.

assertions.value: The lesson states that weak coherent states do not have the desirable quantum properties of single photons, but behave like single photons in many other ways, for example being very low energy and so hard to detect and hard to use for non-linear interactions.
assertions.anchor: Weak coherent states as a testbed and starting point, paragraph 1
quotes: While they don't have the desirable quantum properties, weak coherent states will behave like single photons in many other ways.
they are very low energy and are therefore hard to detect and implement non-linear interactions.
assertions.certainty_reason: The lesson states the limit of weak coherent states directly in this paragraph.

assertions.value: The lesson states that weak coherent states are an excellent tool to understand what can be done and to contribute to developing devices while ensuring scalability, and that they let the team see at an earlier stage of hardware development what works and what does not.
assertions.anchor: Weak coherent states as a testbed and starting point, paragraph 1
quotes: An advantage of relatively easy-to-prepare weak coherent states is that they provide an excellent tool to understand what we can do and to contribute to the development of our devices, ensuring scalability.
We can therefore use these states to understand what works and what doesn't at an earlier stage in hardware development.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor describes its own development method.

assertions.value: The lesson states that nonlinear optics can convert weak coherent states into more quantum states, and that a nonlinear system that starts with weak coherent states can transform them into more interesting quantum states over time.
assertions.anchor: Weak coherent states as a testbed and starting point, paragraph 1
quotes: Additionally, nonlinear optics can also convert weak coherent states into more quantum states.
so a nonlinear system that starts with weak coherent states can transform them into more interesting quantum states over time.
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement in a vendor lesson with no derivation or data on the page.

assertions.value: The lesson states that the nonlinear effects underlying QCi's technology have been experimentally demonstrated by its team to make an excellent source of single photons. The page gives no data for this result and links to it.
assertions.anchor: Weak coherent states as a testbed and starting point, paragraph 1
quotes: The nonlinear effects that provide the foundation of our technology have been experimentally demonstrated by our team to make an excellent source of single photons .
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor describes its own product; the page carries no measurement.
assertions.reader_inference: The page does not say what source quality was measured or how, so the word excellent is unquantified here.

assertions.value: The lesson states that working with weak coherent states makes engineering much easier and allows rapid testing, and that this ability to look ahead lets the team design different elements of its architecture independently and understand encodings and protocols on a large scale early on.
assertions.anchor: Weak coherent states as a testbed and starting point, paragraph 1
quotes: However, working with weak coherent states allows for a setting where engineering is much easier, and allows us to rapidly test what works and what doesn't.
This ability to "look ahead" allows us to design different elements of our architecture independently, and gain an understanding of encodings and protocols on a large scale early on.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor describes its own design process.
